# About the call

The [AGUASAN Community of Practice (CoP)](http://www.aguasan.ch) is an interdisciplinary Swiss community of specialists in the field of water and sanitation within the framework of international cooperation. It meets regularly for knowledge exchange and, among its activities, organises the AGUASAN Workshop Series. **Since 1984, AGUASAN Workshops have been a key forum for experience sharing and knowledge generation** of the Swiss international cooperation in water.[^1] Each edition brings together, over 5 days, up to 50 practitioners from development, humanitarian aid, research, and policy for an intensive week of structured discussion around a single, current topic. Working from real case studies, participants reflect collectively and develop practical approaches, tools, and pathways they can carry back into their own work. Funded by the SDC, AGUASAN Workshops constitute an essential link in the agency's thematic knowledge management strategy and processes.

[^1]: Throughout, water is understood as the broader water and sanitation sector, spanning water supply, sanitation, hygiene, water resources management, and related governance and finance systems.

The overall goal of the [AGUASAN Workshop Series](https://aguasan.ch/workshops) is to forge the implementation of the Swiss response on water issues in international cooperation. For four decades, the workshops have addressed a [broad spectrum of highly relevant practice-oriented sector themes](https://firebasestorage.googleapis.com/v0/b/hazu-ch.appspot.com/o/files%2F9UVMjiOioddwKpmyppzAdEEnuiu2%2FAGUASAN%20Workshop%20Topics%201984-2025_1758639907868.pdf?alt=media&token=69db4bdc-d98b-412c-b6d6-9c817e7dd320), ranging from sanitation and health to the human rights to water and sanitation, the implementation of the SDG6, and circular water and sanitation models, all the way to the most recent 38^th^/39^th^ editions on the WASH Humanitarian-Development-Peace Nexus and Systems Strengthening. These were tackled first from a global perspective (2024, in Switzerland) and then applied to refugee-hosting contexts (2025, in Uganda). In line with orientations from SDC Section Water and latest AGUASAN thoughts, the next and **40^th^ AGUASAN Workshop in the summer of 2027** builds on a preparatory process that is deliberately demand-driven. Hence, the AGUASAN CoP invites its members and the SDC RésEAU to submit **topic proposals**. The selected topic will then determine the workshop's framing, its location (Switzerland or abroad), and the Steering Committee composition.

# What we are looking for

In practice, a proposal puts forward a subject for a five-day AGUASAN Workshop and names an organisation willing to help the workshop process and interested in using its results. **We invite proposals for a timely, sector-relevant topic** suited to this format: a retreat amongst water professionals to share bluntly experiences, successes and learning, and to generate possible pathways to better address the topic in their work.

A strong proposal brings together three elements:

- **A topical and relevant theme for the sector:** a subject that matters now and speaks to a shared concern across the community.
- **A suitable context:** global, regional or local, to anchor the discussions.
- **An institutional champion:** an organisation with a high interest in having the topic addressed.

Each proposal must be linked to a Swiss-based organisation or project, and should identify an organisation - ideally an AGUASAN CoP member - willing to act as **custodian**: to champion the topic, help shape the workshop, and carry its results forward. Where a topic points to a specific country or region, the custodian should be able to connect the workshop to the national or regional actors who would use its outcomes.

# How proposals will be assessed and used

The standing Steering Committee members and its facilitators (backstopper) will review all submissions against their relevance and timeliness, the demonstrated demand within the community, the strength of the proposed custodianship, the clarity of the expected added value, and overall feasibility. The selected topic will be confirmed over the summer, **then deepened at a one-day preparatory event in Switzerland in October 2026** (back-to-back with the CoP meeting). Detailed preparation follows over the winter, with the workshop itself anticipated in 2027.

# How to respond

Please complete the proposal template below and return it to [roger.schmid\@skat.ch](mailto:roger.schmid@skat.ch) by **30 June 2026**. The template is short; you are welcome to attach supporting material. Questions may also be directed to the same address.

**Eligibility:** open to AGUASAN CoP members, SDC RésEAU members, and their partners. Each proposal must however be **linked to a Swiss-based organisation or a Swiss-financed project**; RésEAU members and partners not based in Switzerland are welcome to propose together with their Swiss-based partner organisation or project.

## 2. The proposed topic

### 2.1 Working title \*

> Publishing WASH Data Together: A Hands-On Retreat for an Open, AI-Ready Sector.

### 2.2 Relevance and timeliness \*

*Describe the topic and why it is timely and relevant for the sector. Why does it matter now?*

> The WASH sector is flush with data, from household surveys to theses to published manuscripts, yet it is rarely shared. The result is duplication, fatigue, and waste, with much of what exists locked in reports and PDFs that are quickly lost. Meanwhile AI has moved in a few years from a better search engine to a tool that can analyse data, build apps, and surface research gaps. The question is shifting from "can a machine write this?" to "is our data ready for it?" The real work now is publishing WASH data following FAIR principles and making it AI-ready: openly licensed, well documented, linked, and reproducible. This workshop is a working retreat where every participant arrives with a dataset and leaves having published it, building the skills and mindset to keep their data open, reusable, and AI-ready for the rest of their careers.

## 3. Context and added value

*The workshop location (Switzerland or abroad) will be decided on the basis of the selected topic.*

### 3.1 Preferred setting

*Is the topic best addressed in Switzerland, in a specific country or region, or is it topic-led with no strong preference? If a specific country or region, please specify and explain.*

> Topic-led, with a preference for Switzerland. The hands-on format benefits from a shared cloud environment and stable connectivity, and the topic is global rather than tied to one country. The work already reaches institutions abroad: funded data stewards have been embedded in partner organisations in Malawi and South Africa.

### 3.2 Added value of an AGUASAN workshop in this context \*

*What would be the added value of addressing this topic through an AGUASAN workshop, in the proposed context?*

> The workshop turns a time-limited research-data programme into ongoing sector practice. Between 2023 and 2026, Global Health Engineering at ETH Zurich ran five projects funded by the Open Research Data Program of the ETH Board (roughly CHF 500,000), building the openwashdata community, a data publishing workflow, an online academy, and tools that support an open science culture, work that received the National Prize for Open Research Data 2024, awarded by the Swiss Academies of Arts and Sciences. The funding window closes in 2026; an AGUASAN workshop in 2027 is the natural bridge to carry the effort forward across the sector rather than leaving it to chance.

### 3.3 Who would benefit from the workshop results

*Which national, regional, or international entities would benefit from the workshop's discussions and results, and what link already exists with them?*

> Utilities learn from one another and gain arguments for institutional change at home; NGOs and practitioners make their in-house data visible and reusable; early-career professionals build good data management habits; researchers gain a competitive advantage in their academic career, and senior practitioners adapt to fast-changing tools with less stress. The openwashdata community already links to more than 200 academy registrants, partner organisations in Malawi and South Africa, and a catalogue of 51 documented, reusable datasets.

## 4. Demand, ownership and custodianship

### 4.1 Evidence of demand \*

*What indicates there is interest in this topic, and among which actors?*

> The Data Science for openwashdata course has run twice. The first iteration drew more than 200 registrations and produced 22 final capstone projects; the second drew more than 150 registrations and graduated 48 participants, each publishing a capstone project with a dataset of their choice. Alongside the course, funded data stewards were embedded inside partner organisations in Malawi and South Africa. The appetite for practical, open, reproducible data management skills, from individual learners to institutions, is already demonstrated.
>
> The interest is broad amongst sector professionals: the competencies apply in any context and the skills are transferable, because the workshop relies on free open source tooling that anyone can access without buying costly licenses.
>
> To measure demand directly, we would reuse the pre-courses survey developed for the second iteration of Data Science for openwashdata and published as an open source resource. The survey establishes a detailed baseline of participants' current digital skills, highlighting their specific strengths, gaps, and needs. The anonymised results would contribute to a better understanding of the skills and competencies that exist across the WASH sector.

### 4.2 Envisaged follow-up \*

*How would the workshop's outcomes be taken forward, and by whom?*

> A third iteration of Data Science for openwashdata by the openwashdata academy, a free ten-week online course, would bring AGUASAN workshop participants and their colleagues properly into reproducible-data work by fully equipping them with foundational skills in the R programming language for data analysis. Because the course is open to anyone, it would further the transfer of knowledge and build community between AGUASAN workshop participants and the wider WASH sector. Workshop participants would start with an advantage, having already been exposed to complementary tools such as Git, GitHub, and Quarto. This third iteration would be revised to integrate the use of AI for data science work.
>
> A special issue in a sector journal focused on WASH data papers would give published data a citable home. A more formal home for the sector's open data would build a bridge from "we publish and archive on GitHub and Zenodo today" to a long-term foundation for data publications in the sector. The team overseeing the openwashdata community at ETH Zurich would carry these efforts forward: a permanent full-time position is dedicated to managing the community for long-term sustainability.

## 5. Expected outcomes

### 5.1 What the workshop could produce \*

*What concrete outputs could the workshop deliver (e.g. partnerships, a tool, guidance, a roadmap), who would benefit, and how?*

> This is a working retreat where every participant builds something real. A precondition to attend is bringing a dataset to publish. Before the workshop, the hosts will engage with selected participants to provide individual support in gathering the documentation and permissions needed to publish their datasets.
>
> By the end of the week, 30 to 50 documented data packages exist in at least draft form, ready to be unified and shared through a common GitHub infrastructure. From there, archiving on Zenodo generates a durable DOI and a license defines the usage terms, so that datasets follow FAIR data sharing principles. Participants also leave with a small set of durable skills, Git and GitHub, Quarto, and some exposure to R, along with an understanding of what comes next for the safe use of AI agents. Each participant outlines concrete next steps for integrating these tools into their own organisation.

## 6. Substance the workshop could draw on

### 6.1 Possible case studies

> The 22 capstone projects from the first academy iteration and the 48 capstone projects from the second, each built on a dataset the participant chose and is in the process of publishing, offer ready case studies of practitioners publishing their own data. The data-stewardship work in Malawi and South Africa shows the institutional case. The FAIRqual project provides a harder case: how qualitative materials such as interviews and workshops, which often resist anonymisation, can be shared following FAIR principles while protecting research subjects.
>
> Beyond the academy, several national and city-level initiatives show open WASH data already working at scale, and offer instructive cases for the workshop:
>
> - **Malawi:** mWater has been used to map and assess the quality of approximately 47,000 water points serving 4.8 million people, with the data captured on the platform and openly accessible.
> - **Cape Town, South Africa:** the City publishes weekly dam levels for the Western Cape Water Supply System on its open data portal, including downloadable historical time series. A live public dashboard at [waterdashboard.co.za](https://waterdashboard.co.za) shows current storage, historical trends, and 24-month projections. Because the data is openly licensed and accessible via ArcGIS, third parties can build on it, and they have: [capetowndamlevels.co.za](https://capetowndamlevels.co.za) is one independent site built on the same data.
> - **Kampala, Uganda:** Weyonje ("emptying" in Luganda) is a GIS-enabled mobile app developed by the Kampala Capital City Authority (KCCA) to manage faecal sludge across the city. It was built with GSMA Digital Utilities Innovation Fund support from 2017, in partnership with GIZ and the National Water and Sewerage Corporation.
> - **Finland:** VEETI is Finland's national Water Services Information System, operational since 2016, owned by the Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry and operated by the Finnish Environment Institute (SYKE). It is a compulsory national database for all water and wastewater utilities in the country. Non-restricted data from VEETI is publicly accessible via open APIs through SYKE's environmental data services, so researchers, planners, and third-party developers can query it directly.
>
> Possible speakers include alumni of the Data Science for openwashdata course whose participation led to published, reusable data. One example: Kelsey Shaw began working with her PhD data during the first cohort and, with openwashdata support, published it openly and co-authored a paper in *Environmental Science & Technology*. We would also invite a speaker from PLOS (Public Library of Science), with whom we co-hosted a webinar on FAIR data sharing in January 2023 (Lauren Cadwallader, Open Research Manager), to speak to the publishing and data-paper pathway. A speaker working at the intersection of WASH and AI, such as Olivier Mills of Baobab Tech / WASH AI, could speak to making sector data AI-ready.
